newsitem.title: USA: Western U.S. power market laments generation gap.
newsitem.headline: Western U.S. power market laments generation gap.

text.p: Looking to explain a surprising jump in western U.S. cash power prices, long-time utility traders blamed the influence of inexperienced market players for at least some of the volatility.
"It's a lot different now with all the marketers being involved," a trader at a Portland, Ore.-based utility said.

He referred to a new class of company encouraged by the National Energy Policy Act of 1992 and by Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) efforts to open up access to interstate power transmission lines.
By late March, FERC had approved 292 power marketing companies, including lots of newly-created susidiaries of existing regulated monopoly electric utilities.
FERC certified 157 power marketers last year alone.

The western U.S. has been a focus for many of the new players since a block of 14 states share an interconnected power grid. California has been one of the first states to pursue deregulation, and the New York Mercantile Exchange chose western hubs as delivery points for electricity futures contracts launched just over a year ago.
Spot power prices in the Southwest have more than doubled during the first half of May, following a recent pattern that stubbornly ignores market fundamentals, sources said.

"We aren't buying into the market hype. We would rather go out and run our own generation. Then we can avoid the transmission losses and all the games you have to play," said a California utility trader.
Marketers, however, do not have that option, since they generally do not own or control generating facilities.
As a result, their large trading positions are often covered in the spot market, sources noted.
Edison Electric Institute said this week independent power marketers re-sold 230 million megawatt hours of electricity last year, up 776 percent from 1995.
One trader ascribed the recent market rally to "general hysteria" amid a trading community dealing with the onset of what is forecast to be a hot summer in the western U.S.
But several utility traders said triple-digit temperatures in the Desert Southwest are not unusual this time of year.
"So it's a 100 degrees (Fahrenheit) in Phoenix. Big deal. They plan for that," said one utility market source.

Others noted the Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), which typically has a surplus of power this time of year, has apparently committed itself to selling more power under long-term contracts than it is generating.

BPA, the federal agency which markets large volumes of power produced at hydroelectric dams in the Northwest, made these forward sales commitments earlier in the year when the region was buried under a near-record snowpack.
But flood control and fish migration restrictions so far have limited power generation at many of the projects, according to Bonneville.
As a result, BPA has been a spot buyer rather than a seller this spring, an unexpected state of affairs which has sent players scrambling to cover short positions.
Sources also noted that normal springtime maintenance outages at many of the region's power plants appear to have spooked some market participants.
"People thought May would mean a lot of hydropower, so thermal units were put on maintenance as usual," said an Oregon trader.

But a California trader noted that even if BPA sold all, or even slightly more, than the amount of power being generated at federal hydropower projects, "somebody bought the power so somebody has it."
She noted many of the new marketers have backgrounds in the natural gas industry, but "electricity isn't the same as gas. You can generate power from several products."

Recently, the electricity market "is acting like we're generating on gas, but we're in runoff," the California trader said, noting natural gas prices are more of a factor during dry summer and winter months.
But other sources said lower-than-expected precipitation in California this winter cut into the state's hydropower generating capacity, even as the Northwest grapples with way too much water.

When heavy flooding hit northern and central California early this winter, reservoirs were drawn down to hold even more rain, but precipitation for the rest of the winter was below normal and reservoir water levels ended up slightly lower than usual.
"California doesn't have as much water as we had last year. If there is an extended heatwave, I wouldn't be surprised to see a price spike," said another San Francisco-based market source.
((--Los Angeles bureau + 1 213 955 6761))
